passage: I was hanging clothes on my balcony when the construction crane next door dropped a steel pipe. Clang! Across the gap, little Akash, who is maybe two, froze on his mat, arms flung wide. Then he scrambled backwards on his bottom, bumped into his mother's knees and buried his face in her dupatta. He did not look up again until the workers went quiet. Sonali, his mother, just held him and rocked.

qa.q: What sound made Akash freeze on his mat?
qa.a: A steel pipe dropped by the construction crane next door made a loud clang.

qa.q: What does Akash hiding his face in the dupatta suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He was probably frightened by the sudden noise and wanted the safety of his mother, though the neighbour can only guess from what she saw.

qa.q: What could Sonali do if the building noise keeps startling Akash?
qa.a: She could keep holding him close when loud bangs come, and later name the sound calmly, like 'that was the big pipe', so it feels less strange.

qa.q: How does the neighbour see Akash's reaction?
qa.a: She sees it as a quick, natural startle and notices how fast his mother's rocking settled him.

grounding: Illustrates an instinctive fear reaction in a toddler to a sudden loud noise, seen by a neighbour.

passage:
Monday: Abba switched on the mixer grinder and Zainab screamed, dropped her spoon and ran to the bedroom door, sobbing.
Thursday: Anand, her Abba, held her in the kitchen doorway before switching it on. She pressed her hands over her ears and hid her face in his shirt, but stayed.
The next week, she heard the lid click, covered her ears herself, and watched the chutney whirl from his lap.

qa.q: Where did Zainab run the first time the mixer grinder started?
qa.a: She ran to the bedroom door, sobbing.

qa.q: Why did Zainab scream and run on Monday?
qa.a: The sudden roar of the mixer grinder scared her; her body reacted before she could understand what the noise was.

qa.q: What worked well in how Anand helped her?
qa.a: He did not force her close; he held her at a safe distance and warned her by his presence, so she could get used to the noise bit by bit.

qa.q: What would change if Anand had laughed at her fear or made her stand near the grinder?
qa.a: She might have grown more scared of the kitchen, because her fear would have been pushed instead of calmed. 😟

grounding: Shows a toddler's instinctive fear of a loud machine easing over several days with a caregiver's support.

passage:
"Open wide, Darshan. It's pumpkin."
"No!" Darshan clamped his lips and turned his head.
"Just a tiny taste?" Harsha touched the spoon to his mouth.
He scrunched his nose, pushed out his tongue, and orange mush slid down his chin. "Yucky!"
"Okay, okay." Harsha wiped him. "Not today."
"Nana?"
"You want banana? Here." She put a slice beside the pumpkin on his plate. "The orange one can sit there too."

qa.q: What food did Harsha offer Darshan first?
qa.a: She offered him pumpkin.

qa.q: How can you tell Darshan felt disgust at the pumpkin?
qa.a: He clamped his lips, scrunched his nose, pushed out his tongue and said 'Yucky', which shows the taste or texture felt unpleasant to him.

qa.q: Which part of Harsha's approach might help Darshan accept new foods later?
qa.a: She stopped pushing and gave him a familiar banana, but left the pumpkin on the plate so he can see it again without pressure.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel when Darshan spits out food she cooked?
qa.a: She may feel a little tired or disappointed, but she stays patient and treats it as a normal toddler reaction.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler rejecting an unfamiliar taste with disgust cues, and a calm caregiver response.

passage:
Note for Ayesha's parents, from Deepika (playgroup)
Today we played with cold, wet oats in a tray. Ayesha poked it once, pulled her hand back and shook her fingers hard, making an 'eee' face. She wiped her hand on my kurta and would not go near the tray again. 😅
I gave her a spoon instead, and she scooped from a distance. We will try dry rice next time.

qa.q: What did the children play with in the tray?
qa.a: They played with cold, wet oats.

qa.q: What does Ayesha shaking her fingers and making an 'eee' face suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the slimy, wet feel was unpleasant to her and she wanted it off her skin.

qa.q: Which choice by Deepika helped, and why?
qa.a: Offering a spoon let Ayesha stay in the game without touching the texture she disliked, so she could explore at her own distance.

qa.q: How might Ayesha's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They would likely feel reassured that her dislike was noticed kindly and that the teacher has a gentle plan for next time.

grounding: Shows a toddler rejecting an unpleasant sensory input, recorded in a playgroup teacher's note.

passage:
Childminder's note, Tuesday, by Elizabeth
Nazia's red balloon slipped from her wrist in the garden and floated over the fence. She reached up with both arms, then crumpled onto the grass, crying hard and pointing at the sky. 😢
I sat down beside her and said, 'Your balloon went away. You're sad.' She climbed into my lap. After a while we blew bubbles, and she watched them drift up too.

qa.q: Where did Nazia's red balloon go?
qa.a: It slipped from her wrist and floated over the fence.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when she crumpled onto the grass?
qa.a: She felt sad and upset about losing something she loved, shown by her crying hard and pointing at where it went.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth do that helped Nazia?
qa.a: She sat beside her and named the loss and the feeling in simple words, then offered comfort before moving to a new activity.

qa.q: What might Nazia's parents want to know after reading this note?
qa.a: They may want to know she was comforted and calmed, and that she might still mention the balloon at home. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a toddler expressing unhappiness after losing a desired object, noted by a childminder.

passage: At the temple fair in their kasba, Swati bought her little sister Yamini a paper pinwheel. Yamini ran along the canal bank, holding it high to catch the wind. Then her foot slipped, and the pinwheel dropped into the water. She stood still, lip trembling, watching it float away. A loud wail followed. Swati picked her up, patted her back and pointed at the bangle stall. Yamini kept sniffling into her shoulder.

qa.q: What did Swati buy for Yamini at the fair?
qa.a: She bought her a paper pinwheel.

qa.q: What does Yamini's trembling lip before the wail suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the sadness of losing her new pinwheel was building up in her before it burst out as crying.

qa.q: What else could Swati try if Yamini stays upset?
qa.a: She could say out loud that the pinwheel is gone and Yamini is sad, and let her cry a little before offering distractions.

qa.q: How might Swati feel about the pinwheel falling in?
qa.a: She may feel sorry for her sister and a bit sad herself, since she chose the gift to make Yamini happy.

grounding: Shows a toddler's sadness at losing a wanted object, in a small-town fair setting.

passage:
Evening note from Farida Nani, for Ayesha's Ammi
Today I opened the big black umbrella inside the verandah. Whoosh! Ayesha's eyes went round, her mouth made an 'O', and she fell back on her bottom. Then she laughed and laughed. I closed it and opened it six times, and each time she squealed and clapped. By the end she was pushing the button with me. 🙂

qa.q: How many times did Farida Nani close and open the umbrella?
qa.a: She closed and opened it six times.

qa.q: How can you tell Ayesha felt surprised when the umbrella first opened?
qa.a: Her eyes went round, her mouth made an 'O' and she fell back, which shows the sudden change caught her off guard.

qa.q: What small step made the surprise fun instead of scary?
qa.a: Nani repeated it calmly and let Ayesha push the button, so the unexpected thing became a shared game.

qa.q: What would change if the umbrella had opened right in Ayesha's face without Nani there?
qa.a: The surprise might have turned into fear, because she would not have had a familiar person to show her it was safe.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler reacting to a sudden change with surprise that turns into playful delight.

passage: The local bus bumped along the mustard fields. Simran, not yet two, sat on her sister Anjali's lap by the window. At a stop, a brown goat poked its head right through the bars. Simran gasped and jerked back. The goat bleated. Simran stared, then let out a giggle and reached for its ear. Anjali held her wrist gently and laughed with her until the bus pulled away.

qa.q: What poked its head through the bus window?
qa.a: A brown goat poked its head through the bars.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling when she gasped and jerked back?
qa.a: She was startled by something sudden and unexpected, and her body pulled back before she could decide it was funny.

qa.q: How could Anjali support Simran after such a surprise?
qa.a: She can stay close and calm, name what happened ('a goat came to say hello'), and keep her safe while letting her enjoy it.

qa.q: How might the other passengers see Simran's reaction?
qa.a: They would probably find her gasp turning into a giggle sweet and amusing, a small bright moment on the bus.

grounding: Shows a toddler's surprise at an unexpected event, set on a rural Indian bus.

passage: In the wheat field's shade, Amandeep woke from his nap on the charpai and called out, 'Ammi!' Dilnaz, cutting grass nearby, straightened and waved. 'Here, jaan.' He sat up, sucked his thumb, and watched her. When a buffalo lowed, he called again, and again she answered and came to rub his back. Soon he climbed down and lined up pebbles, glancing now and then to find her still there.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz doing when Amandeep woke?
qa.a: She was cutting grass nearby in the field.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep keep glancing at Dilnaz while he played?
qa.a: He wanted to check she was still there; knowing she would answer made him feel safe enough to play.

qa.q: What does Dilnaz's response show about building trust?
qa.a: Answering every call, even small ones, teaches him that his needs will be met, which lets him explore on his own.

qa.q: What would change if Dilnaz often ignored his calls?
qa.a: He might cling more or cry longer, because he could not be sure she would come when he needed her.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler's growing sense of security from a caregiver who responds consistently.

passage: At two in the morning, rain drummed on the flat's window in Hamburg. Hiroshi woke up and cried. Within a minute Elif was at the cot, her hair messy. 'I'm here. Just rain.' She laid a warm hand on his tummy. He hiccupped, found her finger and gripped it. His eyes closed slowly. Elif stayed a while, then tiptoed out. Hiroshi stirred once, then went back to sleep.

qa.q: What woke Hiroshi at two in the morning?
qa.a: Rain drumming on the window woke him, and he cried.

qa.q: What does Hiroshi gripping Elif's finger suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt comforted and safe with her there, and could relax back into sleep.

qa.q: What is helpful about how Elif responded?
qa.a: She came quickly and calmly and used touch and a few soft words, which is a steady, predictable comfort.

qa.q: What is it like for Elif to get up for these wakings?
qa.a: It may be tiring for her, but she seems to accept it and still stays until he settles. 😴

grounding: Shows a toddler feeling secure because a caregiver reliably meets his needs at night, set in Germany.

passage:
"Mama's home!" Dilnaz called from the door.
Ojas dropped his blocks. "Mama! Mama!" He ran, arms up.
"Oof, such a big hug." She kissed his cheeks.
His uncle held out a biscuit. "Come to Mamu, Ojas?"
"No." Ojas wrapped his legs around Dilnaz and pressed his face into her neck.
"All right, Mamu can wait," she laughed. "You missed me, hm?"
He patted her cheek with a sticky hand.

qa.q: What did Ojas drop when his mother came home?
qa.a: He dropped his blocks.

qa.q: Why did Ojas refuse to go to his uncle?
qa.a: He wanted to stay close to his mother, whom he had missed and prefers when he is tired or excited.

qa.q: How could Mamu respond so he does not feel hurt?
qa.a: He could smile and wait, and play with Ojas later; this preference is normal and not a rejection of him.

qa.q: How might the uncle feel when Ojas says 'No'?
qa.a: He might feel a small pang, but also understand that Ojas simply loves his mother most right now.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler showing warm affection and a clear preference for his primary caregiver.

passage:
Pick-up note by Alka, daycare helper
Arnab had a calm day and ate all his poha. But when his Baba came in at five, Arnab ran across the room shrieking with joy and threw himself at his legs. He kept kissing Baba's hand and would not let me put on his shoes; only Baba could. I stood back. It was lovely to see. 🤍

qa.q: At what time did Arnab's Baba come in?
qa.a: He came in at five.

qa.q: What do Arnab's shrieks and kisses suggest he felt when his father arrived?
qa.a: They suggest deep love and relief at seeing his father, the person he feels closest to.

qa.q: Why was stepping back a good choice for Alka when Arnab refused her help?
qa.a: She stepped back and let Baba help, respecting Arnab's wish to be close to his caregiver instead of taking it personally.

qa.q: How might Arnab's Baba feel reading this note?
qa.a: He would likely feel happy and moved to know how much his son looks forward to seeing him.

grounding: Shows a toddler's warmth and preference for his primary caregiver, recorded by a daycare helper.

passage: On Monday morning at the nursery in Leeds, Bilal's mum kissed him and turned to leave. Bilal grabbed her coat and screamed, face red and wet. Emeka, his key worker, knelt beside him. 'Mummy's coming back after lunch.' Bilal kicked and reached for the closing door. Emeka held him close by the window, and they waved together. Ten minutes later Bilal was sniffling over the toy trains, still holding Emeka's sleeve.

qa.q: Who is Emeka?
qa.a: Emeka is Bilal's key worker at the nursery.

qa.q: Why did Bilal scream when his mum turned to leave?
qa.a: He was frightened and upset to be apart from her, and did not yet trust that she would come back.

qa.q: What could help Bilal on the next mornings?
qa.a: A short, warm goodbye and the same routine each day, like waving at the window with Emeka, can help him learn she always returns.

qa.q: How might Bilal's mum feel walking away from the door?
qa.a: She may feel sad or guilty hearing him cry, even though she knows he will settle with Emeka.

grounding: Illustrates separation distress in a toddler when parted from his parent, set at a nursery in England.

passage: I'm Elizabeth, and my little brother Yash is almost two. On Mum's night-shift days, I watch what happens. When she picks up her bag, he stops playing and follows her to the door. The moment it shuts, he bangs on it and cries 'Mumma!' until his voice cracks. I carry him to the window so he can see her auto leave. He kicks, then goes quiet on my shoulder. I don't know if he understands she's coming back.

qa.q: What does Yash do the moment the door shuts?
qa.a: He bangs on it and cries 'Mumma!' until his voice cracks.

qa.q: What might Yash be worried about when he follows his mother to the door?
qa.a: He seems worried about being apart from her, and may not yet trust that she will return.

qa.q: What could the older sibling try to make these evenings easier?
qa.a: They could keep a small routine, like the window wave and a favourite toy, and say each time that Mum will come back in the morning.

qa.q: How does the older sibling see Yash's crying?
qa.a: They watch it closely and feel responsible, but they are unsure what Yash understands, which shows care mixed with uncertainty.

grounding: Shows a toddler's separation anxiety at a parent's departure, described by an older sibling.

passage:
Playgroup note from Irfan Sir
Today Alka, who is two and a half, did something sweet. When a friend's crayon box fell and scattered, Alka went straight over, picked up every crayon and dropped them back in, one by one. Nobody asked her. Later she handed me my keys when they slipped off the table. 👍 I just said, 'Thank you, Alka,' and she went back to her puzzle.

qa.q: What did Alka hand to Irfan Sir later?
qa.a: She handed him his keys when they slipped off the table.

qa.q: What does Alka going back to her puzzle after being thanked suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she helped because she wanted to, not to get praise or a reward.

qa.q: What did Irfan Sir do well in his response?
qa.a: He thanked her simply without making a big fuss or giving a prize, which keeps the helping her own choice.

qa.q: How might the friend whose crayons fell see Alka?
qa.a: The friend may feel looked after and more likely to see Alka as kind and friendly.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler spontaneously helping by picking up dropped items without being asked.

passage: By the village well, Kishore Dada was washing his face, his gamchha draped on the stone edge. A gust blew it into the dust. Before he could bend, little Devika toddled over, grabbed the cloth in both fists and held it up to him, beaming. 'Dada, lo!' Nobody had told her to. He took it, laughed, and ruffled her hair. She was already running back to chase the hens.

qa.q: What did the gust blow into the dust?
qa.a: It blew Kishore Dada's gamchha off the stone edge into the dust.

qa.q: How did Devika seem to feel about helping Dada?
qa.a: She seemed happy and eager, beaming as she held the cloth up to him without anyone asking.

qa.q: How could adults encourage this kind of helping?
qa.a: They can notice it warmly, as Dada did with a laugh, without turning it into a task or a reward.

qa.q: How does Kishore Dada see what Devika did?
qa.a: He seems touched and amused that such a small child noticed and helped him on her own.

grounding: Shows a toddler assisting an elder without prompt or reward, set in an Indian village.

passage:
"Yamini, bath time's over. Teeth now."
"No teeth!" Yamini flung the brush on the floor and flopped down.
"Hmm." Harsha sat beside her. "Who brushes first, you or Teddy?"
She peeked. "Teddy."
Harsha brushed the bear's fuzzy mouth. "Your turn."
"Me do!" She grabbed the brush and chewed it, grinning.
"Good job. Then story, then sleep."
"Two story!"
"One story, Yamini."

qa.q: Who brushed first before Yamini?
qa.a: Teddy, her bear, got brushed first.

qa.q: Why did Yamini fling the brush and flop down?
qa.a: She did not want to stop playing and resisted the routine, feeling frustrated at being told what to do.

qa.q: Which choice by Harsha worked, and why?
qa.a: Turning brushing into a game with Teddy let Yamini feel in charge, so she joined in instead of fighting.

qa.q: What would change if Harsha had shouted and forced the brush in?
qa.a: Bedtime might have become a battle, and Yamini could start dreading the routine instead of slowly accepting it.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler moving between resisting and accepting a bedtime hygiene routine.

passage:
Weekly crèche note, by Ganga Didi
Omkar is learning 'tidy-up time'. On Monday he threw himself down and kicked when the bell rang. On Wednesday he put two cars in the basket after I sang our clean-up song. Today he carried the whole basket to the shelf himself and looked at me, chest out. 🙂 He still cries when it's time to wash hands, so we are working on that next.

qa.q: What did Omkar do on Monday when the bell rang?
qa.a: He threw himself down and kicked.

qa.q: What does Omkar looking at Ganga Didi with his chest out suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt proud of carrying the basket and wanted her to notice.

qa.q: How could Ganga Didi use what worked for tidy-up with handwashing?
qa.a: She could add a short song or a fun step to handwashing too, since the song helped tidy-up become a routine.

qa.q: How might Omkar's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They may feel encouraged by his progress and understanding about the handwashing crying, since it shows he is still learning.

grounding: Shows a toddler slowly adopting a toy-pickup routine while still resisting handwashing.

passage:
"Trisha, hot! Don't touch." Damini lifted her hand from near the stove.
Trisha's lip wobbled. "Hot?"
"Yes, hot. Ouch. Come play here."
Trisha looked at the flame, then at her mother, and toddled to her pots on the floor.
"Good listening."
When Nani came in with her cane, Trisha dropped the pot and hugged Nani's legs.
"Arre, my little one!"
"Nani sit," Trisha said, pulling her to the chair.

qa.q: Where did Damini lead Trisha to play?
qa.a: She led her to play with her pots on the floor.

qa.q: What does Trisha looking at the flame, then at her mother, suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was unsure but trusted her mother's warning enough to follow it.

qa.q: How could Damini keep encouraging Trisha to accept guidance?
qa.a: She can keep warnings short and clear, give a safe alternative, and praise her for listening, as she did here.

qa.q: How might Nani feel when Trisha hugs her legs and pulls her to the chair?
qa.a: She would probably feel loved and cared for by her granddaughter. ❤️

grounding: Illustrates a toddler accepting a parent's guidance and showing natural affection towards an elder.

passage:
Home-to-daycare diary, from Karthik's father, Pradeep
On Sunday we visited Thatha. When Thatha said, 'Karthik, shoes off inside,' Karthik stopped and pulled at his sandals right away, though at home he fights us about it. He sat close to Thatha all evening and kept patting his knee. At dinner, when I said 'enough sweets,' he pouted but put the laddu down. We were pleasantly surprised.

qa.q: Whom did the family visit on Sunday?
qa.a: They visited Thatha.

qa.q: What might Karthik have felt towards Thatha, based on his behaviour?
qa.a: He seems to feel both respect and warmth for Thatha, since he obeyed him quickly and stayed close, patting his knee.

qa.q: What could the daycare teacher take from this note?
qa.a: She could see that Karthik listens well to calm, trusted adults, and use short, friendly instructions with him.

qa.q: Why might Thatha's words work better than the parents' at home?
qa.a: Karthik may see Thatha as a special elder and be eager to please him, while at home he is testing limits with his parents.

grounding: Shows a toddler deferring to parental and grandparental guidance and showing affection for an elder, in a father's diary note.
